After the death of her father, a wealthy merchant, she used her inheritance in 859 to found the al-Qarawiyyin mosque, named after the immigrants from Kairouan; her sister Maryam is said to have founded the Andalusian mosque at the same time. According to tradition, Fatima fasted throughout the construction. A place of teaching developed at the mosque for the Quran, law, grammar, mathematics and astronomy, where scholars such as Ibn Khaldun later studied or taught; the University of al-Qarawiyyin exists to this day and is often described as the oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning in the world.

name: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
role: Philosopher, judge and physician in al-Andalus
summary: The scholar from Córdoba whose commentaries on Aristotle shaped Christian and Jewish philosophy in the Middle Ages.
text: Ibn Rushd came from a family of legal scholars in Córdoba and himself became chief judge in Seville and Córdoba as well as personal physician to the Almohad caliphs. Besides a medical handbook he wrote short, middle and long commentaries on the works of Aristotle, in which he freed the philosopher's teaching from later additions, and he defended philosophy as the duty of the thinking believer. In 1195 he was charged on account of these views and banished to Lucena, but was rehabilitated shortly before his death in Marrakesh in 1198. In Europe he was so influential under the name Averroes that the church banned the teachings of his followers in Paris in 1277; the Jewish philosopher Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas built on his writings.

name: Jalal al-Din Rumi
summary: The mystic from Konya whose poems on the love of God are among the most widely read works of world literature.
text: Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh in present-day Afghanistan; his family fled westward from the Mongols and settled around 1228 in Konya, the capital of the Seljuks of Rum, from which he took his name. There he worked as a legal scholar and preacher until his meeting with the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz in 1244 made him a poet and a mystic. His main work, the Masnavi with some 25,000 couplets, combines stories, Quranic interpretation and the teachings of Sufism; to this are added thousands of poems on the soul's longing for God. From the circle of his students arose the Mevlevi order, whose dervishes worship God with their whirling dance; his tomb in Konya remains a place of pilgrimage today.

name: Timur (Tamerlane)
summary: The ruler of Samarkand who spread fear with campaigns from India to Anatolia while maintaining a brilliant court.
text: Timur was born in 1336 near Kesh south of Samarkand into a Turco-Mongol tribe; an injury left him with a limp, from which the names Timur Lenk and Tamerlane arose. Since he was not descended from Genghis Khan, he formally ruled in the name of Mongol puppet khans, but saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol empire and a defender of Islam. From 1370 until his death he led campaigns into Persia, Russia, India, Syria and Anatolia that were of extraordinary cruelty toward cities that resisted. In Samarkand he had splendid buildings such as the Bibi-Khanym Mosque erected, and in 1401 he received the historian Ibn Khaldun outside Damascus for long conversations. His descendants, the Timurids, made Samarkand and Herat centers of astronomy, painting and poetry in the 15th century.

name: Ibn Khaldun
role: Historian, statesman and founder of social science
summary: The scholar from Tunis who in his Muqaddimah was the first to examine the laws governing the rise and fall of empires.
text: Ibn Khaldun came from a family of scholars driven out of Seville and was born in Tunis in 1332. As secretary, envoy and minister he served changing rulers in North Africa and Granada, was imprisoned several times, and withdrew in 1375 to a castle in Algeria, where he wrote the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his world history. In it he explained the changing fortunes of empires through the cohesion of groups, asabiyyah: nomadic tribes with a strong sense of solidarity conquer softened cities, lose their own strength there within a few generations, and are replaced by new conquerors. From 1382 he lived in Cairo as a judge and professor at al-Azhar; in 1401 he negotiated with Timur outside besieged Damascus. His study of economy, climate, rule and society is regarded today as a forerunner of sociology and historical scholarship.

name: Konrad Adenauer
role: First chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany
summary: Bound the young Federal Republic firmly to the West and laid the ground for prosperity, sovereignty and reconciliation with France.
text: Adenauer was mayor of Cologne from 1917 to 1933, was removed by the National Socialists and temporarily imprisoned. In 1949, at 73, he was elected the first federal chancellor by a majority of one vote and governed for 14 years. Against fierce resistance he pushed through integration with the West: accession to the Coal and Steel Community and in 1955 to NATO, rearmament, reparations to Israel, and in 1963 the Élysée Treaty with France; in 1955 he secured in Moscow the release of the last German prisoners of war. Critics accused him of sacrificing reunification to the freedom of the West and of tolerating former Nazis in the administration. Germans nevertheless reelected him three times; he stepped down in 1963.

name: Nikita Khrushchev
role: Soviet party leader and head of government
summary: Denounced Stalin's crimes, sent Sputnik into space and faced Kennedy in the Cuban Missile Crisis.
text: The son of a miner rose under Stalin to become party leader of Ukraine and of Moscow and prevailed in the power struggle after Stalin's death in 1953. In a secret speech at the party congress in 1956 he condemned Stalin's terror and cult of personality and released millions of prisoners, but in the same year had the Hungarian uprising crushed with tanks. His policy of peaceful coexistence alternated with threats: in 1958 he issued an ultimatum over Berlin, in 1961 he approved the building of the Wall, and in 1962 he stationed missiles in Cuba, which he withdrew after thirteen days. With Sputnik and Gagarin he won prestige for the Soviet Union, and trouble with failed agricultural reforms. In 1964 the Politburo removed him; he died a pensioner in Moscow.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
role: Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement
summary: Led the nonviolent struggle against racial segregation in the United States and gave the I Have a Dream speech in 1963.
text: King grew up in Atlanta in a family of ministers and became the voice of the Black civil rights movement through the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955. Following Gandhi's example he relied on marches, sit-ins and civil disobedience; arrests, bomb attacks on his house and FBI surveillance did not stop him. Before 250,000 people at the March on Washington in 1963 he invoked his dream of a country in which people are not judged by the color of their skin; in 1964, at the age of 35, he received the Nobel Peace Prize, and the civil rights and voting rights acts of 1964 and 1965 ended legal discrimination. In his last years he fought against poverty and the Vietnam War. On 4 April 1968 he was shot in Memphis.

name: Rosa Parks
role: Civil rights activist in the United States
summary: Her refusal to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger set off the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955.
text: Rosa Parks worked as a seamstress in Montgomery, Alabama, and had been secretary of the local civil rights organization, the NAACP, since 1943, for which she documented cases of violence against Black people. On 1 December 1955 she refused to give up her seat to a white passenger, was arrested and fined; her steadfastness gave the signal for the boycott that brought down segregation on the buses. She lost her job, received death threats and moved to Detroit in 1957, where she worked for decades for a congressman and continued to campaign for civil rights. Congress honored her in 1999 with its highest award; after her death she was the first woman to lie in state in the Capitol.

name: Ho Chi Minh
role: Founder and president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam
summary: Led Vietnam in the struggle for independence against France and into the war against the United States.
text: The son of a scholar left the French colony of Indochina in 1911 as a ship's cook, lived in London, Paris, Moscow and China, and in 1920 was among the founders of the French Communist Party. In 1941 he founded the independence movement Viet Minh, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi on 2 September 1945 and led the war against France, which ended in 1954 with the victory at Dien Bien Phu and the division of the country. As president of North Vietnam he supported the guerrilla struggle in the South and, in the war against the United States, rejected any compromise that gave up the unity of Vietnam. He died in 1969, six years before victory; the captured capital Saigon was named after him in 1976.

name: Deng Xiaoping
role: Reform politician and de facto leader of the People's Republic of China
summary: Opened China to the market economy from 1978 and made it a rising economic power, but had the democracy movement crushed in 1989.
text: Deng encountered communism as a work-study student in France, took part in the Long March and rose to become one of Mao's closest associates. During the Cultural Revolution he was stripped of power twice and banished to work in a tractor factory. After Mao's death he prevailed in 1978 and began the policy of reform and opening: farmers were again allowed to produce for the market, special economic zones such as Shenzhen attracted foreign capital, students went abroad; with the saying that it did not matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice, he justified his pragmatism. In 1984 he agreed with Margaret Thatcher on the return of Hong Kong. He rejected political freedom and in June 1989 had the protests on Tiananmen Square ended with tanks. His course made China the second largest economy in the world within a single generation.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
role: British computer scientist and inventor of the World Wide Web
summary: Developed the World Wide Web at CERN and waived patents so that it would be open to everyone.
text: Berners-Lee, the son of two computer pioneers, studied physics at Oxford and worked as a software developer at the European research center CERN. To link the scattered documents of the physicists, he proposed a system of hyperlinks in 1989 and in 1990 wrote the first browser and the first web server, along with the foundations HTML, HTTP and URL. He ensured that CERN released the technology free of charge in 1993, and in 1994 founded the World Wide Web Consortium, which still sets open standards today. He was knighted for his invention in 2004 and honored with the Turing Award in 2016. For years he has warned about the power of the large platforms and campaigned for the protection of personal data and an open web.

name: Angela Merkel
role: First female chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany
summary: Led Germany from 2005 to 2021 through the financial, euro, refugee and coronavirus crises and shaped European politics.
text: Angela Merkel grew up in East Germany as the daughter of a pastor, earned a doctorate in physics and entered politics only during the peaceful revolution of 1989. Under Helmut Kohl she became a minister, in 2000 leader of the CDU, and on 22 November 2005 the first woman to become chancellor. In sixteen years in office she saved banks and euro states with billions in aid during the financial and euro crises, decided after Fukushima in 2011 to phase out nuclear power, and in 2015 opened the borders to hundreds of thousands of refugees with the words we can do this, which brought her admiration and sharp criticism at home and abroad. During the coronavirus pandemic she explained the situation to citizens in televised addresses. Her policy toward Russia, above all the dependence on Russian gas, was sharply questioned after the attack on Ukraine in 2022.

name: Justinian I
summary: The Byzantine emperor who codified Roman law, built the Hagia Sophia and tried to reconquer the West.
text: Justinian came from a peasant family in the Balkans and succeeded his uncle Justin on the throne in 527. He saw himself as the restorer of the Roman Empire: his generals conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy, his commission of jurists under Tribonian compiled all of Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, and his building program culminated in the Hagia Sophia. He survived the Nika riot of 532 only thanks to the resolve of his wife Theodora. His wars and an outbreak of plague from 541 exhausted the empire, which soon lost most of the conquests again.

name: Theodora
summary: The actress who rose to become the most powerful woman in Byzantium and strengthened the rights of women.
text: Theodora was the daughter of a bear keeper in the circus of Constantinople and performed as an actress, a profession that at the time excluded women from society. Justinian had a law changed specifically so that he could marry her in 525, and he raised her to be co-ruler. When the Nika riot threatened the palace in 532 and the emperor wanted to flee, she declared, according to Procopius, that the purple made a fine shroud, and moved him to stay. She pushed through laws against forced prostitution and in favor of divorced women and protected the persecuted Miaphysites in the east of the empire. Her mosaic portrait in San Vitale in Ravenna is among the most famous works of art of the period.

name: Otto I the Great
summary: The victor at the Lechfeld, whose imperial coronation in 962 marks the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire.
text: Otto was crowned king at Aachen in 936 and prevailed in years of fighting against rebellious dukes and his own relatives. He bound the bishops and imperial abbeys closely to the crown, endowed them with land and sovereign rights and made them the support of his rule. After the victory over the Hungarians in 955 and the founding of the archbishopric of Magdeburg as a base for missions to the Slavs, he marched to Italy and received the imperial crown in 962. His second wife Adelaide and his brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, were important co-rulers; his tomb lies in Magdeburg Cathedral.

name: Thomas Aquinas
summary: The Dominican who sought to unite faith and reason in his Summa Theologica and brought scholasticism to its height.
text: Thomas came from a noble family near Aquino in southern Italy and entered the mendicant order of the Dominicans against the will of his family. He studied under Albertus Magnus in Cologne and Paris, where he later taught himself, and in only two decades produced an enormous body of work, including commentaries on Aristotle and the unfinished Summa Theologica. Unlike many of his contemporaries he held the philosophy of Aristotle, which had reached Europe through Averroes and Avicenna, to be compatible with Christian faith, since for him reason and revelation came from the same source. He died in 1274 on the way to the Council of Lyon; in 1323 he was canonized and his teaching became the foundation of Catholic theology.

name: Eleanor of Aquitaine
role: Duchess of Aquitaine, queen of France and England
summary: The most powerful woman of the 12th century, who married two kings, accompanied a crusade and fostered courtly culture.
text: As heiress to the vast duchy of Aquitaine, Eleanor married the French king Louis VII in 1137 and accompanied him on the Second Crusade in 1147. After that marriage was annulled in 1152 she married Henry Plantagenet, who two years later became King Henry II of England; their combined holdings reached from Scotland to the Pyrenees. At her court in Poitiers the poetry of the troubadours flourished. Because she supported her sons in a revolt against their father, Henry kept her in confinement for fifteen years; after his death she governed for her son Richard the Lionheart and raised the ransom for his captivity. She died at a great age in the abbey of Fontevraud.

name: Frederick II (Hohenstaufen)
role: Holy Roman emperor and king of Sicily
summary: The learned Hohenstaufen emperor whom contemporaries called the wonder of the world and who regained Jerusalem without a blow of the sword.
text: Frederick grew up an orphan in Sicily, where Arab, Greek, Jewish and Latin cultures met, and spoke several languages. Crowned emperor in 1220, he built Sicily into a tightly administered state with the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231 and founded the University of Naples in 1224. On his crusade in 1228 he won Jerusalem through a treaty with the sultan al-Kamil, even though the pope had excommunicated him. He wrote a treatise on falconry based on his own observation and supported poets and scholars. His decades-long struggle with the popes ended only with his death in 1250, and a few years later the Hohenstaufen line died out.

name: Pachacuti
summary: The ninth Inca, who turned the city-state of Cusco into an empire and shaped its administration, roads and buildings.
text: Only oral traditions, recorded by Spanish chroniclers in the 16th century, tell of Pachacuti. According to them he saved Cusco from the Chanka as a young prince, stripped his father Viracocha of power and ruled from about 1438 to 1471. He organized the conquered land into provinces, resettled population groups, introduced the sun cult as the imperial religion and had Cusco laid out anew in the shape of a puma with the sun temple Coricancha. Terraces, canals and roads supplied the growing population, and the royal estate of Machu Picchu is attributed to him. His son Tupac Yupanqui continued the conquests.

name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
summary: The creator of the David, the Sistine ceiling and the dome of St. Peter's, who embodies the High Renaissance like no other.
text: Michelangelo grew up in Florence and as a youth was supported in the household of Lorenzo de' Medici. With the Pietà in St. Peter's and the David he became famous before he was thirty; between 1508 and 1512 he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel with more than 300 figures for Pope Julius II, although he regarded himself above all as a sculptor. Later he created the Last Judgment on the altar wall, planned the Medici Chapel and from 1547 directed the building of St. Peter's, whose dome he designed. He worked until shortly before his death at almost 89.

name: Erasmus of Rotterdam
summary: The most famous scholar of his time, who wanted to reform the church with satire and learning but rejected schism.
text: Born the illegitimate child of a priest, Erasmus entered a monastery but left it and lived as an independent scholar in Paris, England, Italy and Basel. His Praise of Folly of 1511 mocked monks, theologians and popes, and his Greek New Testament of 1516 laid the groundwork for the Bible translations of the Reformation. Although many saw him as a forerunner of Luther, he broke with him in 1524 in his treatise on free will, because he abhorred conflict and violence. To this day he is regarded as a pioneer of tolerance and of European learning.

name: John Calvin
summary: The French reformer whose strict teaching and church order shaped Protestantism in Western Europe and North America.
text: Calvin studied law and theology in France, had to flee as a supporter of the Reformation and published the Institutes, the systematic statement of his teaching, in Basel in 1536. From 1541 he shaped Geneva into a city where church and council jointly watched over faith and conduct; services, schools and moral discipline were strictly regulated, and his opponent Michael Servetus was burned as a heretic in 1553. At the core of his theology was the doctrine of predestination, according to which God has destined people for salvation or damnation. Huguenots, Dutch, Scots and Puritans carried his teaching into the world.

name: Ignatius of Loyola
summary: The Basque nobleman and soldier who became the founder of an order after a wound and led the Catholic renewal.
text: While defending Pamplona in 1521, a cannonball shattered Ignatius's leg; during his recovery he read legends of the saints and resolved to devote his life to God. He studied in Paris, where in 1534 he took a vow with six companions, and in 1540 received confirmation of the Society of Jesus from Pope Paul III. The Jesuits committed themselves to strict obedience to the pope, founded outstanding schools and universities and carried out missions from Brazil to Japan and China. His Spiritual Exercises, a guide to prayer and self-examination, are still practiced today.

name: Suleiman the Magnificent
summary: The sultan under whom the Ottoman Empire reached its greatest power and advanced to the gates of Vienna.
text: Suleiman ruled from 1520 to 1566 and conquered Belgrade, Rhodes, large parts of Hungary after the Battle of Mohács in 1526, and Baghdad; in 1529 he besieged Vienna in vain. His fleets dominated the eastern Mediterranean, and his alliance with France against Charles V made him a player in European politics. In his own empire he was called the Lawgiver, because he reorganized administration, taxation and law; his architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul. His wife Hürrem, a former slave, gained great political influence.

name: Akbar
summary: The most significant ruler of the Mughal Empire, who united India and created a religiously tolerant court.
text: Akbar, a grandson of Babur, came to the throne in 1556 at the age of thirteen and ruled for almost fifty years. Although he himself never learned to read, he had books read aloud to him, assembled a library of thousands of manuscripts and fostered painting, music and architecture. In his House of Worship he debated with scholars of all religions and tried to bridge their differences with a court religion of his own. In the end his empire covered most of the Indian subcontinent and was richer than any state in Europe.

name: Isabella of Castile
summary: The queen who united Spain with her husband Ferdinand, conquered Granada and financed the voyage of Columbus.
text: Isabella prevailed as queen of Castile in a war of succession in 1474 and ruled jointly with her husband Ferdinand of Aragon, with whom she joined the two largest kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula. In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs completed the Reconquista with the conquest of Granada, expelled the Jews from Spain in the same year and relied on the Inquisition founded in 1478. Also in 1492, Isabella gave Columbus the means for his voyage west and thereby secured Spain's access to the Americas. She ordered that the indigenous population must not be enslaved, though in practice this had little effect.

name: Thomas Jefferson
role: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president of the United States
summary: The plantation owner and Enlightenment thinker from Virginia who formulated the ideals of the American Revolution while holding slaves.
text: Jefferson, a lawyer and landowner from Virginia, wrote the draft of the Declaration of Independence in 1776 at the age of 33, with the statement that all men are created equal. As envoy in Paris he witnessed the beginning of the French Revolution in 1789 and advised Lafayette on the Declaration of the Rights of Man; as the first secretary of state and from 1801 as president, he stood for the rights of the individual states and an America of free farmers. In 1803 he bought the Louisiana Territory from France and thereby doubled the area of the United States. A broadly educated architect, inventor and founder of the University of Virginia, he owned slaves all his life, among them Sally Hemings, with whom he had several children; this contradiction with his ideals shapes his image to this day. He died on 4 July 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration of Independence.

name: Marie Antoinette
summary: The daughter of Maria Theresa who as queen became the target of hatred toward the court and died under the guillotine in 1793.
text: The Austrian archduchess was married at 14 to the heir to the French throne in order to strengthen the alliance between Habsburg and Bourbon, and became queen in 1774. Her spending on clothes, festivities and the Trianon estate, the affair of the diamond necklace in 1785 in which she was entangled through no fault of her own, and pamphlets mocking her as a wasteful foreigner made her the most hated woman in France; the remark attributed to her that the people should eat cake is not documented. During the revolution she pressed the hesitant king to resist and in 1791 promoted the failed flight to Varennes as well as secret contacts with Austria. After the fall of the monarchy she was separated from her children, charged with high treason before the revolutionary tribunal and executed on 16 October 1793.

name: Marquis de Lafayette
role: General and politician in America and France
summary: The hero of two worlds, who as a young nobleman fought for American independence and in France argued for a monarchy with a constitution.
text: The 19-year-old marquis sailed to America in 1777 against the will of the court, became General Washington's closest confidant and contributed to the victory at Yorktown. In 1789 he presented the National Assembly with the first draft of the Declaration of the Rights of Man, commanded the Paris National Guard and created the flag of the revolution with the tricolor. As a moderate supporter of a constitutional monarchy he was caught between the fronts: the radicals accused him of protecting the king, and after the fall of the monarchy in 1792 he fled, only to fall into Austrian captivity, from which Napoleon secured his release in 1797. Under Napoleon he withdrew from public life, made a triumphal tour of the United States in 1824 and in 1830 helped Louis-Philippe to the throne, wrapping him in the tricolor on the balcony of the town hall.

name: Klemens von Metternich
role: Austrian foreign minister and state chancellor
summary: The architect of the Vienna order, who sought for four decades to secure Europe against revolution, liberalism and nationalism.
text: Metternich came from a Rhenish noble family that fled to Vienna before the French revolutionary armies, and in Habsburg service rose to become ambassador in Paris and, in 1809, foreign minister. He arranged Napoleon's marriage to the emperor's daughter Marie Louise, brought Austria over to the allies in 1813 and shaped the Congress of Vienna with the aim of a balance among the great powers. After 1815 he organized surveillance of the press, universities and associations through the Carlsbad Decrees, the German Confederation and congresses of the Holy Alliance; for liberals his name became the very emblem of oppression. The March Revolution of 1848 forced the 74-year-old chancellor to flee to England; he returned in 1851 and died in Vienna in 1859.

name: Miguel Hidalgo
role: Priest and leader of the Mexican independence uprising
summary: The father of the Mexican nation, whose Cry of Dolores in 1810 set off the struggle for independence.
text: Hidalgo, the son of an estate manager, was an educated priest who read Rousseau, promoted workshops and viticulture in his parish of Dolores and spoke with indigenous farmers in their own language. When a conspiracy against Spanish rule was betrayed, he rang the church bells on 16 September 1810 and called for an uprising; under the banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe an army of as many as 80,000 people followed him, took the city of Guanajuato and committed massacres of Spaniards. Before Mexico City he hesitated, was defeated near Guadalajara in January 1811, captured while fleeing north, stripped of his office by the church and shot in Chihuahua on 30 July 1811. His call for the abolition of slavery and of tribute made him Mexico's national hero.

name: Heinrich Friedrich Karl vom und zum Stein
summary: The imperial baron who launched the Prussian reforms in 1807 and became Napoleon's most implacable opponent in Germany.
text: Stein came from a family of imperial knights in Nassau and served Prussia from 1780 as an administrative official and finally as minister; because of his criticism of the cabinet system he was dismissed in January 1807. After the defeat at Tilsit the king recalled him in October 1807, and within a year Stein pushed through the emancipation of the peasants, the municipal ordinance and a reorganization of the ministries in order to involve citizens in administration. When an intercepted letter revealed his hope for an uprising against France, Napoleon forced his dismissal at the end of 1808 and outlawed him; Stein fled to Austria and in 1812 to Russia, where he urged Tsar Alexander to war against Napoleon. In 1813 he organized the administration of the liberated territories, called in vain for a German nation-state and in 1819 founded the Monumenta Germaniae Historica for the study of the Middle Ages.

name: Mary Wollstonecraft
role: English writer and pioneer of women's rights
summary: The author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, who in 1792 demanded equal education and civil rights for women.
text: Wollstonecraft grew up in an impoverished family with a violent father, worked as a companion, teacher and governess, and from 1787 made her way in London as a translator and author, which was unusual for a woman of her time. In response to the French Revolution and to Rousseau's view that women were destined to be educated to please men, she published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792: women appeared weaker and more superficial only because education was withheld from them; she called for coeducational schools, professions of their own and political representation. From 1792 to 1795 she experienced the Reign of Terror in Paris, had a daughter out of wedlock and described her journey to Scandinavia. She died in 1797 a few days after the birth of her daughter Mary, the later author of Frankenstein. In the 19th century her work became a foundation of the women's movement.

name: Spartacus
role: Gladiator and leader of a slave revolt
summary: The Thracian gladiator who led the largest slave revolt of antiquity from 73 to 71 BC.
text: Spartacus came from Thrace in present-day Bulgaria, probably served in Roman auxiliary troops and was sold as a prisoner to the gladiator school at Capua. In 73 BC he escaped with about 70 companions and led a rapidly growing army of slaves and farm laborers that defeated several Roman armies; the sources praise his shrewdness and his fairness in distributing plunder. His aim of crossing the Alps and releasing the slaves to their homelands foundered on his followers' wish to go on plundering Italy. In 71 BC he fell in battle against Crassus; his body was never found. Since the 18th century he has been a symbol of the struggle for freedom.

name: Cleopatra VII
summary: The last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, who allied herself with Caesar and Antony and with whose death her country fell to Rome.
text: Cleopatra came to the throne at 18 and held her own against her brother and co-ruler by winning Caesar to her side in 48 BC; their son Caesarion was to secure the dynasty. She was highly educated, the first Ptolemy to speak Egyptian along with eight other languages, and ruled a rich but Rome-dependent country. After Caesar's death she allied herself with Mark Antony, to whom she bore three children, and shared rule over the East with him. After the defeat at Actium and Octavian's entry into Alexandria she took her own life in 30 BC, by legend through the bite of a snake; Egypt became a Roman province.

name: Livia Drusilla
summary: Wife of Augustus and mother of Tiberius, who for more than five decades was the most powerful woman in Rome.
text: Livia married Octavian in 38 BC, who took her from her first husband although she was pregnant. In 52 years of marriage she became the closest adviser of Augustus, received envoys, managed a great fortune with estates and brickworks of her own, and was regarded as the model of the virtuous Roman matron who wove the emperor's clothing herself. At the same time she secured the succession for Tiberius, her son from her first marriage; rumors that she poisoned rivals are unproven but shaped her image down to Robert Graves's novel I, Claudius. Augustus adopted her in his will as Julia Augusta; her grandson Claudius had her raised to the status of a goddess in 42.

name: Nero
summary: The last emperor of the house of Augustus, notorious for matricide, the fire of Rome and the first persecution of Christians.
text: Nero became emperor in 54 at the age of 16, after his mother Agrippina had probably poisoned the emperor Claudius. Guided by the philosopher Seneca he governed moderately at first, but then had his mother killed in 59 and his wife Octavia in 62. During the great fire of Rome in 64, which devastated ten of the fourteen districts, he was accused of arson; he directed suspicion onto the Christians and had them cruelly executed, and on the ruins he built his enormous palace, the Domus Aurea. Nero performed as a singer, poet and charioteer and toured Greece, which outraged the senators. When governors and praetorians rose against him he took his own life in 68 with the words what an artist dies in me; the Year of the Four Emperors followed.

name: Trajan
summary: The best emperor in the judgment of the Senate, under whom the empire reached its greatest extent.
text: Trajan was born in Italica near Seville in Spain, the first emperor from a province, and was adopted in 97 by the aged Nerva. As a commander he conquered Dacia and campaigned against the Parthians as far as the Persian Gulf. In Rome he used the spoils to build the Forum of Trajan with markets, libraries and Trajan's Column, built harbors, roads and aqueducts in the provinces and created with the alimenta a fund to support poor children in Italy. His correspondence with the governor Pliny shows how he attended to details of administration and did not have Christians actively persecuted. The Senate gave him the title Optimus Princeps, best of rulers; centuries later new emperors were still wished to be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan.

name: Marcus Aurelius
summary: The philosopher on the imperial throne, who fought Germanic peoples on the Danube and wrote his Meditations.
text: Marcus Aurelius was adopted by the emperor Antoninus Pius and succeeded him on the throne in 161, at first jointly with Lucius Verus. His reign was marked by crises: a war against the Parthians, a plague carried in from the East that killed millions, and from 166 invasions by the Marcomanni and Quadi that reached northern Italy forced him to spend years in camp on the Danube. There he wrote the Meditations in Greek, notes of a Stoic on duty, transience and composure, which are among the most widely read books of antiquity. He died in 180 at Vindobona, today's Vienna, or at Sirmium; with his son Commodus the age of the adoptive emperors ended. His equestrian statue on the Capitol is the only surviving one of a Roman emperor.

name: Hypatia of Alexandria
summary: The most famous scholar of late antiquity, who taught in Alexandria and was murdered by a Christian mob.
text: Hypatia was the daughter of the mathematician Theon, the last known scholar of the Museion of Alexandria, and in the judgment of her contemporaries she surpassed her father. She wrote commentaries on the works of Diophantus and Apollonius and on the tables of Ptolemy, built astrolabes and, as head of a Neoplatonic school, taught philosophy to pagans and Christians alike; her student Synesius became a bishop. As an adviser to the city prefect Orestes she was drawn into his power struggle with Bishop Cyril. In March 415 a crowd of Christian fanatics dragged her from her carriage, killed her in a church with shards and burned her body. Her death is regarded as a symbol of the end of ancient scholarship and of the conflict between faith and reason.

name: Homo habilis
summary: The handy human, one of the oldest species of the genus Homo, associated with the first stone tools.
text: Homo habilis was described in 1964 by Louis Leakey and his colleagues from finds in the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania; the name means handy human, because the Oldowan tools were attributed to it. It lived about 2.4 to 1.6 million years ago in East Africa, stood only about 1.20 meters tall and had a brain roughly half the size of that of people today, but distinctly larger than that of the australopithecines. Whether it was a direct ancestor of Homo erectus or a side branch is disputed among researchers.

name: Homo erectus
summary: The first human species with a human-like body, which left Africa, made hand axes and used fire.
text: Homo erectus, the upright human, arose in Africa just under two million years ago. With long legs, short arms and a height of up to 1.80 meters, it was an enduring walker and hunter. The Turkana Boy from Kenya, an almost complete skeleton from 1.6 million years ago, is its best known fossil. Homo erectus developed the hand axe, mastered fire by at least 400,000 years ago and lived in Africa, Europe and Asia; on Java the last groups survived until about 110,000 years ago. Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens probably descend from it.

name: Denisovans
summary: A sister species of the Neanderthals that lived in Asia and was discovered only in 2010 through DNA analysis.
text: In 2010, researchers at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig succeeded in recovering the genome of a previously unknown human species from a tiny finger bone from Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains. The Denisovans were related to the Neanderthals and lived in Siberia, on the Tibetan plateau and probably in Southeast Asia as well. Fossils are rare: a lower jaw from Tibet, a few teeth and bones. Their genetic legacy lives on, however, since people today in New Guinea, Australia and parts of East Asia carry up to five percent Denisovan DNA, including a gene variant that helps Tibetans live at high altitude.

name: Homo floresiensis
summary: The hobbit of Flores, a human species only about a meter tall on an Indonesian island.
text: In 2003, archaeologists discovered in the Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores the remains of people who were only about 1.06 meters tall and had very small brains. Nevertheless they made stone tools, hunted dwarf elephants and probably used fire. The species lived from at least 100,000 to about 50,000 years ago and disappeared around the time Homo sapiens reached the region. It probably descended from Homo erectus or an even older human form that became smaller on the island through insular dwarfism.

name: The Woman of Peștera Muierii
role: Fossil of an early Homo sapiens in Europe
summary: A woman's skull about 35,000 years old from Romania, whose genome offers insight into the first modern humans in Europe.
text: In the cave of Peștera Muierii, the Cave of the Women, near Baia de Fier in Romania, the skull of a woman who lived about 35,000 years ago was found in 1952. She is among the oldest known modern humans in Europe and lived at a time when Neanderthals still inhabited the continent. In 2021 her genome was decoded: it shows high genetic diversity and a Neanderthal component of about three percent. The study proves that the first Europeans were by no means a small, impoverished group, as had long been assumed.

name: Kennewick Man
role: Skeleton of an early inhabitant of North America
summary: A skeleton about 9,000 years old from the US state of Washington, over which a long dispute broke out between science and Indigenous tribes.
text: In 1996, an almost complete skeleton of a man who had died about 8,900 years ago at around the age of 40 was found on the bank of the Columbia River near Kennewick. He was about 1.70 meters tall, had a healed spear point in his pelvis and lived on fish and game. Whether he should be studied scientifically or buried according to the wishes of the Indigenous tribes was fought over in court for years. In 2015 a DNA analysis showed that he is closely related to the Indigenous people of the region today; in 2017 the man, called the Ancient One by the tribes, was ceremonially laid to rest.

name: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg
role: Officer and leading figure of the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944
summary: The severely wounded colonel placed the bomb in Hitler's headquarters and was shot the same night.
text: Stauffenberg came from the Swabian nobility, was shaped by Catholicism and influenced by the poet Stefan George. As a young officer he welcomed parts of National Socialist policy, but the crimes against Jews and civilians in Poland and the Soviet Union and the looming military catastrophe led him to the resistance. In April 1943 an air attack in Tunisia cost him an eye, his right hand and two fingers of his left. As chief of staff to the commander of the reserve army he had access to Hitler's situation briefings from 1944 and took on the assassination himself, even though he also had to lead the coup in Berlin. After it failed he was shot shortly after midnight in the courtyard of the Bendlerblock; his last cry is said to have been for a sacred Germany.

name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
summary: Opposed National Socialism as a pastor, joined the conspiracy against Hitler and was executed a few weeks before the end of the war.
text: The son of a Berlin psychiatrist was a lecturer in theology at 24 and in 1933 was among the first to protest publicly against the exclusion of Jews from the church. He became a leading figure of the Confessing Church and directed its illegal preachers' seminary at Finkenwalde until the Gestapo closed it. In 1939 he returned to Germany from the safety of the United States, because he wanted a voice after the war only if he had shared the ordeal with his people. Through his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnanyi he worked for the military intelligence service Abwehr, which served as cover for the resistance, and helped Jews escape to Switzerland. He was arrested in April 1943; in prison he wrote the letters that became famous as Letters and Papers from Prison. After 20 July, material that was found incriminated him severely, and on 9 April 1945 he was hanged in the Flossenbürg concentration camp on Hitler's express order.

name: Oskar Schindler
role: Businessman and rescuer of about 1,200 Jews
summary: The Nazi party member and war profiteer saved about 1,200 Jewish forced laborers from murder in his factories in Kraków and Brünnlitz.
text: Schindler came from Zwittau in Moravia, joined the Nazi party in 1939 and after the invasion of Poland took over an enamelware factory in Kraków, where he employed Jewish forced laborers because they were cheaper. The businessman became a rescuer: with bribery, alcohol and good connections to the SS he arranged for his workers to be considered indispensable and spared from deportation out of the Płaszów camp of the notorious commandant Amon Göth. When the factory had to be relocated in 1944, he and his wife Emilie compiled a list of about 1,200 names whom he took with him to Brünnlitz in Moravia; there his plant deliberately produced unusable ammunition until the end of the war, and Emilie Schindler cared for sick prisoners. After the war Schindler failed in business in Argentina and Germany and lived on the support of those he had saved. Yad Vashem honored him as Righteous Among the Nations, he was buried in Jerusalem at his own wish, and Steven Spielberg's film Schindler's List made his story known worldwide in 1993.

name: Charles de Gaulle
role: French general and leader of Free France
summary: Called from London in 1940 for the fight to continue, led Free France and later founded the Fifth Republic.
text: The career officer from Lille had argued in vain in the 1930s for a modern armored force and had only just been appointed general and under-secretary of state in June 1940 when the government sought an armistice. He flew to London and on 18 June 1940, in a BBC radio address, called on the French to continue the fight, for France had lost a battle but not the war. From a few thousand volunteers he built the forces of Free France, won the colonies in Africa to his cause and in 1943 united the Resistance inside the country under his leadership. In August 1944 he entered Paris at the head of the liberators and led the provisional government until 1946. In 1958 he returned to power during the Algerian crisis, created the Fifth Republic with a strong president and governed until 1969; he sealed the reconciliation with Germany in 1963 together with Konrad Adenauer.

name: Erwin Rommel
role: Field marshal and commander of the Afrika Korps
summary: The Desert Fox, celebrated by Nazi propaganda, was forced to take his own life after 20 July 1944.
text: Rommel, a Württemberger, had distinguished himself as a daring officer in the First World War and became a favorite of the dictator through his book Infantry Attacks and as commander of Hitler's escort battalion. In the western campaign of 1940 he drove the 7th Panzer Division forward so quickly that it was called the Ghost Division; from 1941 he commanded the Afrika Korps and captured Tobruk in 1942, for which he was made the youngest field marshal. Goebbels's propaganda turned him into a popular hero, and even the British admired the Desert Fox. After the defeat at El Alamein and the Allied landing in Normandy, whose defense he was to organize, he lost faith in victory and had contact with the conspirators of 20 July without taking part in the attempt himself. When his name came up in interrogations, Hitler gave him the choice in October 1944 between the People's Court and poison; Rommel took his own life and received a state funeral with the lie that he had died of his wounds. Historians today see him in more nuanced terms than the myth of the decent soldier: he was a gifted field commander who served the regime loyally until late.

name: Hirohito
summary: Revered as a divine tenno, he presided over Japan's expansionist policy and himself announced the surrender in 1945.
text: Hirohito came to the throne in 1926 and gave his reign the name Showa, enlightened peace. Under the constitution he was supreme commander and a god in human form; in practice he largely left politics to the government and the military, who led Japan into Manchuria in 1931, into China in 1937 and into war against the United States in 1941; his personal responsibility for war decisions and war crimes remains disputed to this day. After the atomic bombs and the Soviet declaration of war he pressed for surrender within a divided leadership and on 15 August 1945 spoke by radio for the first time to his people, who had never heard his voice. The American occupation under General MacArthur refrained from prosecuting him in order to keep Japan stable; in 1946 Hirohito declared that he was not a god and under the new constitution became a symbol of the state without political power. He reigned until his death in 1989 as the longest-serving emperor of Japan and saw the country rise to become an economic power.

name: Alan Turing
summary: Broke the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park and laid the theoretical foundations of the computer.
text: In 1936, as a 24-year-old mathematician in Cambridge, Turing described an imagined machine capable of solving any computable task, and with it created the theoretical model of the computer. From 1939 he worked at the British secret center Bletchley Park, where, building on the earlier work of Polish cryptologists, he designed the electromechanical bombe that determined the daily settings of the German Enigma cipher machine. In 1941 his section cracked the radio traffic of the U-boats, which allowed the Allies to route convoys around the German wolf packs; by some estimates the decryption shortened the war by years and saved hundreds of thousands of lives, but it remained secret for decades. After the war Turing designed computing machines and in 1950 formulated the Turing test for artificial intelligence. In 1952 he was convicted for his homosexuality and forced to undergo hormone treatment; in 1954 he died of cyanide poisoning, probably by suicide. The British government apologized in 2009, and in 2013 he was pardoned.
